new_statements.quote: Stress is automatically assigned to the initial vowel of every lexical root in nouns, verbs, adjectives, numerals, pronouns, and associative particles. All other syllables are unstressed. Stressed vowels are louder and a bit longer than unstressed ones. Pitch, the phonetic manifestation of phonemic tone, is unaffected by stress. There are several correlates of the stressed/unstressed distinction in Moghamo: (1) Consonant alternation i.e. weakening does not occur in stressed syllables. It occurs in all unstressed syllables except for C2 in CVCV verbs ... (4) Stressed vowels are never elided.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress is automatic and morphologically placed: the first vowel of every lexical root (noun, verb, adjective, numeral, pronoun, associative particle) is stressed; prefixes, suffixes and all other syllables are unstressed. Stress is independent of tone; it is cued by loudness and length, by the blocking of consonant weakening in stressed syllables, by vowel centralisation and shortening in unstressed syllables, and by non-elision of stressed vowels.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned in the visible snippets ('All other syllables are unstressed').
new_statements.exceptions: Consonant weakening also fails to apply to C2 of CVCV verbs (historical *CVC-CV); otherwise none visible.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level (lexical root); stated for Batibo Moghamo, not for Ngamambo. Text seen only through Google Books snippets, so wording gaps ('..') and the page are unverified.
new_statements.identity_note: The only stress statement found is Stallcup 1978's description of Batibo Moghamo (Glottolog dialect mogh1246 of Meta' meta1238, ISO mgo), not of Ngamambo (ngam1267, nbv). Ngamambo (Mbu, Santa sub-division) is a closely related Momo variety (88% lexical similarity with Meta' per Wikipedia/Ethnologue; Stallcup and the Longacre volume call it 'the Ngamambo variety of Moghamo'); Akompab 2008 describes the 'Mbit dialect'. The Ngamambo-specific sources that were opened (Achiri-Taboh 2014, Nyindem & Tah 2023, Boyd 1989 on the A&H 1976 tone data) are tone/morphology work silent on stress.

tone_statements.quote: Tones also play a distinctive role in the Ngamambo language. The H, L, M, HL, and LH tones are attested in this language, and the mid-tone is not marked. The H and L tones are commonly marked, and the contour tones are derived from tonological processes (usually, a floating tone from a deleted segment that spreads or docks to the preceding or following sound). These tones are expressed on monosyllabic, disyllabic, and polysyllabic words, and they equally bring about a difference in the meaning of words in the language.
tone_statements.summary: 3 level tones H, M, L + derived contours HL, LH (floating-tone docking); lexical tone; prefix tone predictable by prefix shape (CV=H, V=M, N=L); no stress statement.
